To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we developed a risk score that predicts in-hospital cardiovascular death after PCI and that the risk score also predicts long-term cardiovascular death.

a simple risk score based on five clinical variables (Killip classification, unsuccessful PCI, diabetes mellitus (DM), age >70 years and contrast-induced nephropath (CIN)) may be useful to identify high-risk patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarct (STEMI) who are treated with primary PCI.

the Killip class, the procedural result, the occurrence of contrast induced nephropathy, the presence of diabetes, and the age are independently and strongly associated with the in-hospital cardiovascular death in patients treated with primary percutaneous intervention.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effect of the risk factors in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarct (STEMI).
the development of a risk score to predict in-hospitale cardiovascular mortality in patients treated with primary percutaneous intervention for ST-elevation acute myocardial infarctions.
the development of a clinical score that can be applied to patients with ST-elevated myocardial infarctions treated with primary percutaneous intervention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this risk score could help to identify patients who are at high risk of death and therefore could be candidates for early invasive management.
the risk score developed from five risk predictors readily available after intervention may be useful to identify patients who are at higher risk for short- and long-term mortality.
the risk of a cardiovascular disease event is increased with the presence of the following risk factors: smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia, family history, diabetes and obesity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk score could be a useful tool to stratify patients for risk after primary PCI.
our risk score is a useful tool to predict in-hospitals and long-term mortality after primary PCI.
a risk score for in-hospital and post-discharge mortality after primary PCI could be developed and validated.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the risk of cardiovascular death in patients treated with primary percutaneous intervention for ST-elevation is not only related to the presence of comorbidities, but also to the procedure itself, as reflected by Killip class, unsuccessful procedure and contrast-induced nephropahy.
a simple risk score can be used to identify patients who are at a higher risk of in-hospital and late mortality after primary percutanoeous coronary intervention.
a simple clinical risk score can be used to stratify patients after primary PCI into different risk strata, which can be useful to guide patient management and clinical research.
